description.text: The left humerus is the long bone of the arm between the shoulder and elbow. Its expanded ends provide joint surfaces, while its shaft supplies extensive muscle and fascial attachments. The proximal end consists of a rounded head and adjacent tubercles; the distal end widens into the elbow condyle and epicondyles. These regions must be distinguished from the shaft when assessing orientation or an injury.

The head faces medially, superiorly and somewhat posteriorly toward the glenoid. The lesser tubercle is anterior; the greater tubercle is lateral. The large olecranon fossa is posterior at the distal end. Taken together, these features establish anatomical orientation; apparent screen left or right alone does not establish bone laterality.

The shaft changes from a more rounded proximal profile to a triangular distal profile. Three surfaces and three borders organize its muscle attachments. Distally, the articular trochlea is medial to the capitulum; the epicondyles are non-articular projections flanking this joint surface. Fossae above the articular region accommodate the forearm bones during elbow movement.

classification.text: Long bone of the appendicular skeleton. A compact-walled shaft surrounds the medullary canal, while the expanded ends contain cancellous bone beneath a cortical covering.

location.text: The left arm lies distal to the pectoral girdle and proximal to the forearm. The humeral head meets the scapula; the distal condyle meets the radius and ulna.

structureAndFunction.text: The bone acts as a lever for shoulder and elbow movements and anchors muscles acting on the shoulder, elbow, forearm and wrist. Its shaft separates major anterior and posterior muscle attachments; its joint surfaces transfer forces between the upper limb and the shoulder girdle.

attachments.text: At the proximal end, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle; subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major attach respectively to the lateral lip, floor and medial lip of the intertubercular groove.

Deltoid inserts on the deltoid tuberosity; coracobrachialis inserts medially on the shaft. Brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus. The humeral triceps heads originate posteriorly, separated in part by the radial groove. Biceps crosses the bone without a humeral insertion.

The distal epicondylar regions provide common forearm muscle origins and elbow collateral-ligament attachments. The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach along the corresponding distal shaft ridges, contributing to the boundaries of the arm compartments.

articulations.text: The head articulates with the scapular glenoid at the glenohumeral joint. At the elbow, the capitulum articulates with the radial head and the trochlea with the ulnar trochlear notch.

clinicalNotes.text: Surgical-neck trauma can affect the axillary nerve, producing deltoid weakness and sensory disturbance over the lateral shoulder. A humeral-shaft lesion can affect the radial nerve and weaken wrist and finger extension. These are anatomical correlations; deficits depend on lesion level.

Shaft injuries require attention to the radial nerve and nearby profunda brachii vessels. Examination includes distal circulation and motor/sensory function, with the injury pattern and associated lesions interpreted by a qualified clinician. This atlas does not diagnose a fracture or determine treatment.

facts.text: Identify the medially directed head, anterior lesser tubercle and posterior olecranon fossa together. The left/right identity is stored in the canonical source mapping and is not inferred from camera perspective.
The proximal humerus receives circumflex humeral arterial contributions from the axillary system. Nutrient and periosteal vessels derived from brachial and profunda brachii branches supply the shaft.
The relative contributions to the humeral head are not captured by a single arterial label; injury and surgical exposure can disturb this regional vascular network.

The humerus forms by endochondral ossification: a cartilage model is progressively replaced by bone. The shaft develops before its epiphyseal regions; growth plates separate developing ends from the diaphysis during growth.

detailedSections.title: Ossification

facts.text: The classical eight-centre scheme comprises the shaft, head, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, capitulum, trochlea and the two epicondyles. The olecranon belongs to the ulna and must not be counted as a humeral centre.

Gray (1918) describes fetal shaft ossification followed by separate postnatal proximal and distal centres and later fusion. Its exact appearance/fusion ages are historical observations, not validated age-estimation rules for current patients. Modern skeletal maturation varies and requires age-, sex- and population-appropriate evidence.

detailedSections.reviewNote: A consulted modern indexed overview inconsistently includes the olecranon among humeral centres. This conflict is not silently copied. Contemporary quantitative timing needs review.

facts.text: A supracondylar process may project from the distal anteromedial humerus. A fibrous connection to the medial epicondyle can relate to median-nerve or brachial-artery compression. The cited dry-bone study is a sample observation, not a universal prevalence estimate.

A supratrochlear aperture is a variable opening through the septum between coronoid and olecranon fossae. It should not be confused with a normal nutrient foramen or assumed to exist in this individual source mesh.

The distal medial and lateral epicondyles provide palpable, non-articular reference points on either side of the elbow. The more proximal humerus lies beneath muscle and should be interpreted using its relationships to the shoulder and arm, not treated as uniformly subcutaneous.

description.text: The right humerus is the long bone of the arm between the shoulder and elbow. Its expanded ends provide joint surfaces, while its shaft supplies extensive muscle and fascial attachments. The proximal end consists of a rounded head and adjacent tubercles; the distal end widens into the elbow condyle and epicondyles. These regions must be distinguished from the shaft when assessing orientation or an injury.

The head faces medially, superiorly and somewhat posteriorly toward the glenoid. The lesser tubercle is anterior; the greater tubercle is lateral. The large olecranon fossa is posterior at the distal end. Taken together, these features establish anatomical orientation; apparent screen left or right alone does not establish bone laterality.

The shaft changes from a more rounded proximal profile to a triangular distal profile. Three surfaces and three borders organize its muscle attachments. Distally, the articular trochlea is medial to the capitulum; the epicondyles are non-articular projections flanking this joint surface. Fossae above the articular region accommodate the forearm bones during elbow movement.

classification.text: Long bone of the appendicular skeleton. A compact-walled shaft surrounds the medullary canal, while the expanded ends contain cancellous bone beneath a cortical covering.

location.text: The right arm lies distal to the pectoral girdle and proximal to the forearm. The humeral head meets the scapula; the distal condyle meets the radius and ulna.

structureAndFunction.text: The bone acts as a lever for shoulder and elbow movements and anchors muscles acting on the shoulder, elbow, forearm and wrist. Its shaft separates major anterior and posterior muscle attachments; its joint surfaces transfer forces between the upper limb and the shoulder girdle.

parts.text: The rounded proximal articular region faces the glenoid cavity. Its margin is delimited by the anatomical neck, separating the smooth head from the tubercles.
parts.name: Head

parts.text: A groove bordering the head and providing attachment to the shoulder joint capsule. It is proximal to the surgical neck and should not be used as a synonym for it.
parts.name: Anatomical neck

parts.text: The lateral proximal prominence bears superior, middle and inferior tendon impressions for supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor respectively.
parts.name: Greater tubercle

parts.text: The anterior proximal prominence receives subscapularis. The intertubercular sulcus separates it from the greater tubercle.
parts.name: Lesser tubercle

parts.text: The narrowing immediately distal to the tubercles connects the proximal expansion with the shaft. It is anatomically distinct from the rim around the head.
parts.name: Surgical neck

parts.text: The shaft has three surfaces and three borders. Its proximal and distal shape differ, and the deltoid tuberosity and radial groove interrupt an otherwise continuous cortical surface.
parts.name: Body

parts.text: The distal articular complex includes the capitulum laterally and trochlea medially. Adjacent fossae and epicondyles are important neighbouring features, rather than interchangeable names for these joint surfaces.
parts.name: Condyle

surfaces.text: The shaft surface between the anterior and lateral borders includes the deltoid tuberosity. Distal to this attachment it contributes to the origin of brachialis.
surfaces.name: Anterolateral surface

surfaces.text: The shaft surface between anterior and medial borders includes the continuation of the intertubercular region, a coracobrachialis insertion area and a distal brachialis origin area.
surfaces.name: Anteromedial surface

surfaces.text: The radial groove crosses this region. The lateral head of triceps originates superior to the groove and the medial head principally inferior to it.
surfaces.name: Posterior surface

surfaces.text: The boundary between the two anterior shaft surfaces descends from the greater-tubercle crest toward the coronoid fossa; it is related to pectoralis major insertion proximally and brachialis attachment distally.
surfaces.name: Anterior border

surfaces.text: The boundary between anteromedial and posterior regions extends toward the medial epicondyle. Distally it contributes to the medial supracondylar ridge and attachment of the medial intermuscular septum.
surfaces.name: Medial border

surfaces.text: This boundary between anterolateral and posterior surfaces descends toward the lateral epicondyle, becoming the lateral supracondylar ridge distally. The radial groove crosses its middle region.
surfaces.name: Lateral border

landmarks.text: The rounded lateral distal articular prominence meets the fovea of the radial head. Its articular surface is mainly anterior and inferior.
landmarks.name: Capitulum

landmarks.text: The pulley-shaped medial distal articular surface fits the trochlear notch of the ulna and extends onto the anterior, inferior and posterior aspects of the distal bone.
landmarks.name: Trochlea

landmarks.text: The groove between the proximal tubercles accommodates the tendon of the long head of biceps. Its floor and two lips have distinct muscle attachments.
landmarks.name: Intertubercular sulcus

landmarks.text: The lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus provides insertion for pectoralis major and continues toward the anterior shaft border.
landmarks.name: Crest of greater tubercle

landmarks.text: The medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus receives teres major. Latissimus dorsi attaches in the floor of the groove rather than on this crest.
landmarks.name: Crest of lesser tubercle

landmarks.text: A roughened lateral mid-shaft insertion area for deltoid. It provides an orientation landmark and a useful reference when describing shaft attachments.
landmarks.name: Deltoid tuberosity

landmarks.text: An oblique posterior shaft groove related to the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels. Triceps origins lie on either side of this region.
landmarks.name: Radial groove

landmarks.text: The larger medial distal projection gives attachment to the common flexor origin and ulnar collateral ligament. The ulnar nerve passes behind it.
landmarks.name: Medial epicondyle

landmarks.text: The lateral distal prominence gives attachment to the common extensor region and radial collateral ligament of the elbow.
landmarks.name: Lateral epicondyle

landmarks.text: The anterior depression above the trochlea receives the coronoid process of the ulna as the elbow flexes.
landmarks.name: Coronoid fossa

landmarks.text: The small anterior depression above the capitulum accommodates the radial head during elbow flexion.
landmarks.name: Radial fossa

landmarks.text: The large posterior distal depression accommodates the olecranon during elbow extension. A thin septum separates it from the anterior coronoid fossa.
landmarks.name: Olecranon fossa

landmarks.text: A distal continuation of the medial border associated with the medial intermuscular septum and neighbouring muscle origins.
landmarks.name: Medial supracondylar ridge

landmarks.text: The distal lateral ridge gives attachment to brachioradialis superiorly, extensor carpi radialis longus inferiorly and the lateral intermuscular septum.
landmarks.name: Lateral supracondylar ridge

attachments.text: At the proximal end, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle; subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major attach respectively to the lateral lip, floor and medial lip of the intertubercular groove.

Deltoid inserts on the deltoid tuberosity; coracobrachialis inserts medially on the shaft. Brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus. The humeral triceps heads originate posteriorly, separated in part by the radial groove. Biceps crosses the bone without a humeral insertion.

The distal epicondylar regions provide common forearm muscle origins and elbow collateral-ligament attachments. The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach along the corresponding distal shaft ridges, contributing to the boundaries of the arm compartments.

articulations.text: The head articulates with the scapular glenoid at the glenohumeral joint. At the elbow, the capitulum articulates with the radial head and the trochlea with the ulnar trochlear notch.

clinicalNotes.text: Surgical-neck trauma can affect the axillary nerve, producing deltoid weakness and sensory disturbance over the lateral shoulder. A humeral-shaft lesion can affect the radial nerve and weaken wrist and finger extension. These are anatomical correlations; deficits depend on lesion level.

Shaft injuries require attention to the radial nerve and nearby profunda brachii vessels. Examination includes distal circulation and motor/sensory function, with the injury pattern and associated lesions interpreted by a qualified clinician. This atlas does not diagnose a fracture or determine treatment.

facts.text: Identify the medially directed head, anterior lesser tubercle and posterior olecranon fossa together. The left/right identity is stored in the canonical source mapping and is not inferred from camera perspective.
The proximal humerus receives circumflex humeral arterial contributions from the axillary system. Nutrient and periosteal vessels derived from brachial and profunda brachii branches supply the shaft.
The relative contributions to the humeral head are not captured by a single arterial label; injury and surgical exposure can disturb this regional vascular network.

The humerus forms by endochondral ossification: a cartilage model is progressively replaced by bone. The shaft develops before its epiphyseal regions; growth plates separate developing ends from the diaphysis during growth.

detailedSections.title: Ossification

facts.text: The classical eight-centre scheme comprises the shaft, head, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, capitulum, trochlea and the two epicondyles. The olecranon belongs to the ulna and must not be counted as a humeral centre.

Gray (1918) describes fetal shaft ossification followed by separate postnatal proximal and distal centres and later fusion. Its exact appearance/fusion ages are historical observations, not validated age-estimation rules for current patients. Modern skeletal maturation varies and requires age-, sex- and population-appropriate evidence.

detailedSections.reviewNote: A consulted modern indexed overview inconsistently includes the olecranon among humeral centres. This conflict is not silently copied. Contemporary quantitative timing needs review.

facts.text: A supracondylar process may project from the distal anteromedial humerus. A fibrous connection to the medial epicondyle can relate to median-nerve or brachial-artery compression. The cited dry-bone study is a sample observation, not a universal prevalence estimate.

A supratrochlear aperture is a variable opening through the septum between coronoid and olecranon fossae. It should not be confused with a normal nutrient foramen or assumed to exist in this individual source mesh.

The distal medial and lateral epicondyles provide palpable, non-articular reference points on either side of the elbow. The more proximal humerus lies beneath muscle and should be interpreted using its relationships to the shoulder and arm, not treated as uniformly subcutaneous.

description.text: The left radius lies on the thumb side of the forearm in anatomical position. A small proximal head and neck lead into a curved shaft that expands substantially at the wrist. The bone articulates with the humerus and ulna proximally, with the ulna distally and with the carpal region.

The proximal head has a superior articular depression and a smooth circumference. Below the neck, the radial tuberosity provides a biceps attachment. The shaft has anterior, posterior and lateral surfaces and an interosseous border facing the ulna. Distally, carpal facets and the ulnar notch face different articulating structures.

classification.text: Long bone of the appendicular skeleton.

location.text: Left forearm, between elbow and wrist.

structureAndFunction.text: Rotation at the radioulnar joints allows the radius and attached hand to move around the ulna during pronation and supination. The expanded distal end provides an important load-bearing interface with the carpus.

description.text: The left ulna is the medial forearm long bone in anatomical position. Its large proximal end forms the principal bony hinge with the humeral trochlea. In contrast with the radius, the shaft narrows toward a comparatively small distal head and styloid.

The olecranon and coronoid process bound the trochlear notch. A separate radial notch on the lateral proximal end articulates with the radial head. The shaft has anterior, posterior and medial surfaces, an interosseous border facing the radius and a readily accessible posterior border. An articular disc separates the distal ulna from direct carpal articulation.

classification.text: Long bone of the appendicular skeleton.

location.text: Left forearm, between elbow and wrist.

structureAndFunction.text: The proximal ulna provides elbow stability while its relationship to the radius permits forearm rotation. Muscle and membrane attachments integrate both bones rather than allowing either shaft to function in isolation.

parts.text: The expanded proximal end contains the olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear notch and radial notch.
parts.name: Proximal end

parts.text: The shaft tapers distally and has three surfaces and three borders.
parts.name: Body

parts.text: The small distal head articulates with the ulnar notch of the radius and relates inferiorly to the articular disc.
parts.name: Head

surfaces.text: The anterior shaft provides origins for flexor digitorum profundus and, in its distal part, pronator quadratus.
surfaces.name: Anterior surface

surfaces.text: The posterior surface supplies separate attachment regions for anconeus, supinator and several deep extensor muscles.
surfaces.name: Posterior surface

surfaces.text: The broad upper medial surface gives origin to flexor digitorum profundus; the distal medial region becomes subcutaneous.
surfaces.name: Medial surface

surfaces.text: This edge separates anterior and medial surfaces, extending from the coronoid region toward the styloid.
surfaces.name: Anterior border

surfaces.text: This edge extends from the posterior olecranon toward the distal bone and provides a shared fascial attachment line.
surfaces.name: Posterior border

surfaces.text: The lateral shaft edge anchors the interosseous membrane and faces the radius.
surfaces.name: Interosseous border

landmarks.text: The proximal posterior process receives triceps and enters the humeral olecranon fossa during extension.
landmarks.name: Olecranon

landmarks.text: The proximal anterior projection contributes to the trochlear notch and enters the humeral coronoid fossa in flexion.
landmarks.name: Coronoid process

landmarks.text: The large proximal articular concavity embraces the humeral trochlea.
landmarks.name: Trochlear notch

landmarks.text: The lateral proximal articular surface receives the radial head circumference; its margins relate to the annular ligament.
landmarks.name: Radial notch

landmarks.text: An anterior roughened area distal to the coronoid process receives part of brachialis.
landmarks.name: Ulnar tuberosity

landmarks.text: The distal medial projection is distinct from the adjacent articular head.
landmarks.name: Styloid process

attachments.text: Triceps inserts on the olecranon and brachialis on the coronoid/tuberosity region. Flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus arise from anterior/medial shaft regions. The interosseous membrane attaches to the lateral border.

articulations.text: The trochlear notch meets the humeral trochlea. The proximal radial notch and distal head articulate with the radius at separate radioulnar joints. An articular disc intervenes between the distal ulna and carpus.

anatomicalRelations.text: The other forearm bone is linked on the same anatomical side; the interosseous membrane connects their facing shaft borders.
anatomicalRelations.label: Left radius

clinicalNotes.text: Forearm injury assessment includes associated radial-head and radioulnar-joint lesions. An ulnar fracture with proximal radial dislocation is a different injury pattern from an isolated shaft fracture.

evidence.locator: Introduction: proximal ulna fracture with radial-head dislocation

facts.text: The olecranon and posterior ulnar border are superficial bony reference points. Their relationship changes with elbow position, while the deeper articular notch cannot be assessed by simply viewing the skin contour.
The classical pattern comprises a shaft centre and proximal/distal epiphyseal centres. Fusion and appearance timing require contemporary validation before clinical use.
